assumptions.title: Electricity tariff used to convert lost kWh into ₹
assumptions.why: Assumed value, configurable as TARIFF_INR_PER_KWH in engine/config.py (re-run the pipeline after changing it). Shown on the website as "assumed tariff — see About".
assumptions.source: Rounded value between recent Indian solar tariffs: SECI 2 GW solar + 1 GW/4 GWh storage tender, lowest bid ₹2.86/kWh ([Power Peak Digest, 17 Oct 2025](https://powerpeakdigest.com/seci-auction-discovers-lowest-tariff-for-2-gw-solar-with-1-gw-4-gwh-storage/)) and SECI rooftop solar auction, ₹3.34–4.65/kWh ([Indian Infrastructure, 17 Dec 2025](https://indianinfrastructure.com/2025/12/17/seci-announces-auction-results-for-6-25-mw-rooftop-solar-auction/)).

assumptions.title: Plant 1 DC_POWER divided by a scale factor
assumptions.why: In daylight Plant 1 AC÷DC was 0.0979 (physically impossible) vs 0.9787 for Plant 2. We assume the inverters are similar and the DC sensor/logging was ~10.001× too large.

assumptions.title: Share of inverter-days Isolation Forest treats as unusual
assumptions.why: Isolation Forest needs an expected share of odd days; we have no labels to measure it. Used only for the optional 'unusual day' hint, never for alerts.

assumptions.title: Projected annual loss if faults are not fixed
assumptions.unit: days scaled from the observed period
assumptions.why: Estimate: 34-day loss scaled to 365 days, assuming the rest of the year behaves like May–June and nothing is fixed. Real yearly sunlight and fault patterns will differ.

assumptions.title: Clear-sky sunlight learned from our own data
assumptions.why: No cloud sensor and no plant GPS location, so we cannot use a physical sun model. For each time of day we take the 95th percentile of sunlight over all 34 days (smoothed over 5 readings) as 'what a clear sky gives'. If a time of day was cloudy on almost every day, the reference there would be too low.

assumptions.title: Heat loss = power a 25 °C panel would make − expected power
assumptions.why: Panels are rated at 25 °C. Each plant's temperature coefficient is measured from healthy, sunny rows (efficiency vs panel temperature, straight-line fit). Hot panels and strong sun happen together, so the coefficient is an estimate. If a fit is ever outside the believable range [-0.8, -0.15] %/°C, the typical -0.4 %/°C is used.
assumptions.source: Computed from the data (engine/weather_temperature.py); typical range from silicon panel datasheets

losses.tariff_note: ₹ values use an assumed tariff (ASSUMPTION — see About) chosen between recent SECI auction prices, configurable in engine/config.py.
losses.projection_note: Estimate: 34-day loss scaled to 365 days, assuming the rest of the year behaves like May–June and nothing is fixed.

validation.method: Faults injected into healthy test-day data (clean inverter-days), detected with the same detector and thresholds.
validation.caveat: Healthy days were chosen as days where the default detector raised no alert, so false alarms at default thresholds are optimistic (near 0 by construction). The real false-alarm rate cannot be measured without labelled faults.
validation.soiling_note: Soiling is tested on Plant 1 only (the only plant with inverters healthy on every test day) and on a 10-day window. Its false alarms are Plant 2 inverters whose output trends down within those 10 days; on the full 34 days the same rule raised no degradation alert.

method.note: Clear-sky reference is learned from the 34 days (ASSUMPTION), not a physical model.

temperature.healthy_rows_rule: real reading, sunlight ≥ 0.3 kW/m², not an obvious outage, within ±10% of neighbouring inverters

plant_1.verdict: Inside the typical crystalline-silicon range (-0.5 to -0.3 %/°C). It holds up: in 3 of 4 narrow sunlight bands, hotter panels still give less power. Why it can differ from a datasheet: hot panels and strong sunlight happen at the same time, so the fit also picks up other midday effects (sun angle, inverter limits), and there is only one panel-temperature sensor for the whole plant.

costliest_heat_day.summary: Panels reached 61 °C at 1:15 PM — heat cost about 11% of today's energy (24,750 kWh, ₹74,251 at the assumed tariff); 6.25 h above 50 °C.

plant_2.verdict: Inside the typical crystalline-silicon range (-0.5 to -0.3 %/°C). It does NOT hold up well: in only 1 of 4 narrow sunlight bands do hotter panels give less power, so for this plant the number is weak evidence. Why it can differ from a datasheet: hot panels and strong sunlight happen at the same time, so the fit also picks up other midday effects (sun angle, inverter limits), and there is only one panel-temperature sensor for the whole plant.

breakdown.method: Clear-sky potential = power at 25 °C with the actual sunlight (Phase W2) + cloud loss. Cloud loss = (clear-sky sunlight − actual sunlight) × the plant's power per unit of sunlight at 25 °C. Other = the remainder, so the parts always add up to actual energy.

validation_weather.method: Does knowing the weather make fault detection better? A fair before/after test (Phase W4). Same seeded injections in both versions.
validation_weather.rule: Under a difficult sky (Overcast, or variability ≥ 0.2) for at least 50% of its readings, an underperformance event must last ≥ 1.5 h OR be at least 50% below its neighbours.
validation_weather.caveat: Clean days are days with no alert at default thresholds, so false alarms at default are ~0 by construction; the sensitive setting shows how the rule behaves when clouds DO cause alerts. Without official fault labels we cannot tell which real alerts are false.
validation_weather.verdict: DO NOT KEEP the weather-aware rule: false alarms on clean test days 59 → 35 (default + sensitive thresholds), injected faults lost: 13.

fault_classifier.method: Random Forest classifier trained on faults we planted into healthy inverter-days (early days), tested on planted faults from later days it never saw.
fault_classifier.caveat: Trained and tested on planted faults: real faults can look messier. The AI diagnosis is a second opinion; the rule-based detector still decides which alerts are raised.

model_updates.method: Both models start from the first 10 days. Each later day is predicted before the model sees it; the retrained model then learns that day too.
